english_translation: To divide a thing is the same as to destroy it, and thus we cannot take away from anything its own natural unity in such a way that its being would nevertheless remain in its integrity. The whole is not its parts, but that one thing which emerges from the parts, as Aristotle teaches in First Philosophy, Book VIII.
exegesis:
[VERIFIED] Pico grounds being in unity: division is destruction (*dividere* = to fragment into non-being). A thing cannot lose its unity while retaining integrity of being—to divide is to destroy. [INFERRED] Applied to angelology: seraph's perfection = absolute unity with divine will (no internal division, no multiplicity of competing desires); demon's privation = fracture from divine unity (will against divine order, intellect against truth).

The philosophical function is to establish unity as the measure of being: higher creatures possess greater unity (simpler, more integrated toward single divine purpose); lower creatures involve multiplicity and division. Matter exemplifies multiplicity; seraph exemplifies unity; demon exemplifies division from unity. [VERIFIED] This resolves the paradox: demon retains minimal being (still an angel) but through privation of unity—a quasi-being of division.

[INFERRED] Heptaplus describes the six days creating graduated unity; demonic rebellion as cosmic dissonance. Commento emphasizes seraphim's perfect unity of love and intellect. Oration describes human soul's struggle to maintain integrated unity against divisive ambition and vice. Being & Unity grounds it: unity is being; division is toward non-being.
metaphysical_theme: Unity as the ground of being and integrity; the seraph exemplifying perfect unity with divine will; demons exemplifying division from divine unity and descent toward non-being

notes: HARVESTER passage U.4.2 provides the metaphysical principle underlying the seraph-demon opposition: unity vs. division. The seraph is unified—intellect and will one in devotion to God. The demon is divided—will turned against divine order, intellect against truth. This passage explains why Pico's ethics always emphasizes unity of virtue: virtue is unified orientation of all faculties toward God; vice is their division. The passage thus connects metaphysics and ethics: the hierarchical universe and the virtuous soul mirror each other in their structure of unified participation vs. divisive privation.
